name: Polymarket
tagline: A prediction market where people trade shares in the outcome of real world events.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. No subscription: the business model is trading activity and fees, and you bring your own capital.

verdictSummary: You can build the software in an afternoon: order book, shares priced 0 to 1, a resolution button, a portfolio view. What you cannot build is anyone on the other side of your trade. A prediction market with one participant is a spreadsheet where you argue with yourself, and the entire point of Polymarket is that thousands of people with money at risk are collectively pricing the thing you want to know. Add to that real settlement, a dispute-resolved oracle, custody of actual funds, and the regulatory posture required to let strangers bet money, and the software is the cheap part. Build the forecasting journal instead, it is genuinely useful and it does not need a crowd.
coreLoopDIY: A local play-money prediction tracker where you post your own questions, log probability estimates over time, resolve them, and get scored on calibration.
requirements: Local SQLite file, no accounts, no cloud
whatYouLose: Counterparties, so no price discovery and no market-implied probability
Real money at risk, which is the only reason market prices mean anything
Settlement and a dispute-resolved oracle for ambiguous outcomes
The breadth of live markets: elections, sports, macro, weekly news noise
Mobile app, wallet plumbing, and the ability to actually cash out
moatNotes: Liquidity is the product. Everything else is a website attached to it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody pays Polymarket for the interface. They show up because other people with money are already there, which is what turns a page of buttons into a probability, and because the platform takes custody, handles settlement, and resolves disputed outcomes so you do not have to trust a counterparty personally. A self-hosted clone inherits none of that. It inherits the buttons.
notes: The exchange UI is a weekend; the crowd betting real money is not. The moat is marketplace liquidity plus the custody and resolution machinery that makes strangers willing to post capital.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user forecasting journal and calibration tracker. It is NOT a market, there are no counterparties, no real money, no wallets.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router, TypeScript) with Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, single file ./data/forecasts.db
- Recharts for charts
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost, no auth, no accounts, no telemetry, no external API calls

Data model:
- question: id, text, category, created_at, close_date, resolution_criteria (free text), status (open|resolved|void), outcome (0 or 1, nullable)
- forecast: id, question_id, probability (0.01 to 0.99), stake (play-money points), rationale, created_at
- a question can have many forecasts over time; the latest is your current belief

Features, in scope:
1. Create a question with explicit resolution criteria and a close date.
2. Log a new probability for any open question, with a short rationale. Keep full history.
3. Question detail page: line chart of your probability over time, annotated with rationales on hover.
4. Resolve a question as YES, NO, or void.
5. Scoring page: Brier score overall, by category, and by time bucket. Calibration plot bucketing forecasts into 10 probability bins, showing predicted vs actual frequency, with counts per bin.
6. Play-money ledger: each forecast stakes points at the logged odds, settled on resolution. Show running balance. Points are fake and clearly labeled as fake.
7. Dashboard: open questions sorted by soonest close date, overdue-to-resolve list, headline Brier score.
8. JSON export and import of everything.

Explicitly out of scope: order books, other users, real currency, blockchain, oracles, email, deploy config.

Seed the database with 12 example questions across categories so the charts are not empty on first run. Write a README with setup in under 10 lines and one paragraph explaining how to read a calibration plot.
